title: Jacopo Bertran and Berenguer Ripoll’s portolan chart
summary: The vellum chart shows the Mediterranean and northeastern Atlantic, with wind marks, cities and Atlas mountains.
limit: A prominent inland picture does not identify a marked sailing path or the sounding depth.
firstAction: Set the practice wind marks above the coastal line.
firstView: The outward-arrow reader keeps the channel’s edge separate from the drawn mountain.
secondAction: Set the town marker above the landing strip.
secondView: The shore reader can find the town without counting the height of its picture.
returnEvidence: The new quay sketch puts a large hill sticker above a tiny jetty. Its artist gave the hill space to help a lookout, and the porter still needs a landing label.
high: Carry the marked coast line to Anwen’s seaward post.
low: Fit the landfall label on the lower handover rail.

title: Arnald Domenech’s vellum portolan chart
summary: The chart includes winds, towns, landforms and religious illustrations on one coloured vellum sheet.
limit: A drawing can express a text tradition or mark a named place. Its purpose must be read before using it as geographic evidence.
firstAction: Set apart the drawing key and the water direction lines.
firstView: The route line remains clear after the picture is put back beside its own key.
secondAction: Set a two-part placard for the coastline reader.
secondView: The drawing stays visible, and the nearby harbour entry has its own tagged line.
returnEvidence: A runner has treated every ink mark on a new quay plan as a post. Guide them to a usable reference without hiding the mark meant for a different reader.
high: Send the line with the turn mark circled.
low: Put the picture and the harbour entry on paired clips.

title: Guilio di Cesare Petrucci’s water-damaged portolan chart
summary: The museum records extensive water damage on the sheet. Several rivers in northern Africa remain visible.
limit: An unreadable place on a damaged sheet remains an absence of legible evidence.
firstAction: Place the blank patch over the imitation water mark.
firstView: The practice reader can trace to the edge of the stain. The line beyond it has no surviving ink.
secondAction: Put the unchanged section past the dry side mark.
secondView: The remaining ink lines give one usable route segment. The spoiled corner stays covered.
returnEvidence: The coast crew's copy of a mooring board lost one line to damp. Anwen can use the intact mark while the unknown step stays open.
high: Take the legible leg to the north check point.
low: Fit the open gap into the lower runner’s record.

title: Portolan chart attributed to Pedro or Jorge Reinel
summary: The manuscript is drawn on two vellum sheets joined together. The catalogue notes a latitude scale and the uncertain maker attribution.
limit: A repeated line across a seam reveals something about the chart. It cannot choose between two makers.
firstAction: Bring the split paper scale across both halves of the exercise.
firstView: The scale continues across the matched seam. The maker slip still carries two names.
secondAction: Raise the second flap and check the facing edge.
secondView: The line joins across both paper halves. The little signatures remain marked as catalogue attributions.
returnEvidence: Anwen has received two wet slips with a matching drawn bearing. The name is on another leaf. Keep the join and the writer search separate.
high: Carry the matched seam as a provisional quay view.
low: Fit the two leaves and writer gap on the handover clip.

title: Nicholas Comberford’s chart of Hispaniola
summary: The Hispaniola chart is mounted on two hinged boards and has a distance scale in Spanish leagues.
limit: A scale for a unit must travel with any distance copied from it.
firstAction: Unfold the study chart until the scale is accessible.
firstView: The practice line takes three units on its own scale strip. The units remain printed below it.
secondAction: Fold back one panel and carry the scale strip separately.
secondView: A second reader can recover what the line’s divisions meant even when half the model is folded.
returnEvidence: A keeper needs the scale tag after a page is folded for travel. Attach it before the shortened view goes into the working drawer.
high: Take the complete scale and route across the pier.
low: Fit the portable half with the separate scale key.

title: Third book of John Seller’s English Pilot
summary: The catalogue lists eleven uncoloured charts and notes that the volume ends abruptly on page 24.
limit: A planned continuation is not a surviving instruction or a verified route.
firstAction: Follow the illustration flag to the final printed leaf.
firstView: The practice sequence ends after one part. The next fold is a blank space.
secondAction: Put an open marker beyond the printed end.
secondView: The reader sees exactly where evidence stops and leaves the next route unchecked.
returnEvidence: An old route folder ends before the local ferry entrance. The steward wants to circulate the completed part without inventing what was left out.
high: Take the finished first part to the open post.
low: Fit a hanging blank for the unchecked part.

title: Léon Brault’s first-quarter probable-wind chart
dateKind: both years listed by the catalogue
summary: This North Atlantic chart describes likely wind strengths and directions during January, February and March and documents its own construction.
limit: Likely winds for a quarter do not establish weather during one actual watch.
firstAction: Clip the quarter flap to the distribution strip.
firstView: The pattern gives a broad tendency. It still lacks an entry for the current watch.
secondAction: Clip a lookout’s local strip to the separate today half.
secondView: The local mark has its own time and can disagree with the probable quarter.
returnEvidence: The Slate Harbour watch needs its local wind note even if the keeper already has a seasonal pattern.
high: Carry the broad reading beside its quarter label.
low: Take the watch card to a second point and record the difference.

title: J. Cheevers’s printing of Cook’s Tahiti chart
summary: The engraved chart of Tahiti includes a miles scale and sparse soundings. The catalogue names the 1773 voyage account as its publication.
limit: Scattered soundings identify particular observation places. They do not establish all points between them.
firstAction: Lay a transparent frame over the three drawn sounding marks.
firstView: The three marked places sit apart. The blank water between has no digit.
secondAction: Place the proposed cross-bay trace across the same frame.
secondView: One stretch crosses a blank area. The check stops at the last marked depth.
returnEvidence: A harbour runner needs a route to a tray. The practice chart has gaps, so a witness can mark an open question instead of labelling every step checked.
high: Pin the three marked checks under the date and place strip.
low: Set the next possible check beside the blank reach.

title: I. Bayley’s 1772 printed chart of New Zealand
summary: The engraving gives Endeavour’s track from October 1769 through April 1770 as well as a graduated frame.
limit: The ship's track records a voyage from one crew’s viewpoint and does not show every coastal route or local name.
firstAction: Clip the dated track on its own transparent strip.
firstView: The line follows the named voyage between its dates. The land still has places outside the line.
secondAction: Pin a separate collection place to the quiet shore edge.
secondView: Its pin remains fixed as the strip passes. The printed track gives no visit record for it.
returnEvidence: The crew wants to tell visitors which journey its model records. The coast has another name board from the people who use the nearer steps.
high: Take the one dated voyage strip to the lookout.
low: Fit both the land marker and the track on separate pegs.

title: Halifax radio-transmitted North Atlantic weather chart
summary: The record names the Canadian Forces Meteo Centre in Halifax and the 22 December 1974 chart, with a geostrophic wind scale.
limit: Its transmitted chart is bounded by its issue time, region and conditions. One inferred wind field is not a local observer's reading.
firstAction: Slot the model's weather line under its time strip.
firstView: This named issue can be filed. The older issue beside it retains its separate time.
secondAction: Bring the independent lookout’s marker into the same frame.
secondView: The hand marker gives one quay observation, and its time remains separate.
returnEvidence: The quay watched one shift after the issued chart. Someone can compare them only if both times travel.
high: Take the radio issue and region to the lookout frame.
low: Fit the later hand reading separately on the runner’s rail.

title: U.S. Coast Survey island reconnaissance and sketch sheet
summary: Two named coastal subjects appear on the same transfer-lithograph sheet. The artist and source credits are listed separately.
limit: Bound together on one sheet does not mean the views depict one location or one observer.
firstAction: Clip the Smith’s or Blunt’s Island label over the practice sheet’s upper view.
firstView: The second island retains its own place label even while the paper stays one piece.
secondAction: Lift the Anacapa tab and raise the printed maker strip.
secondView: The names of artists and mapped places now sit on different rails.
returnEvidence: Someone receiving the sheet needs to use the view facing the right headland. The keeper can preserve two place IDs on one folio.
high: Take one clearly named view to the upper lookout.
low: Keep both indexed views on the handover rail.

title: Marshallese navigation chart given by Solomona Tuatagaloa
summary: The museum describes shells for islands and separate typed place-name strips. It attributes the chart to a Marshallese maker and records the giver by name.
limit: The public description gives named materials and custody. It does not supply the complete procedures of Marshallese navigators.
firstAction: Set the catalogue place-name tags in a paper folder beside their custody slips.
firstView: The maker entry stays Marshallese. The donor and place of handover remain on their own lines.
secondAction: Place an empty practice place tag on the invented quay grid.
secondView: The generic model gets its own place name. The historical chart has not been traced or copied.
returnEvidence: A fictional carrier brings a labelled object through two ports. Keep her note where a reader can see the difference between a maker and a giver.
high: Take a named handover line to the lookout’s catalogue slot.
low: Fit the maker and donor slips as separate indexed records.

title: Tin signal flag game
summary: The game uses two revolving spinners with compass roses, apertures and thirty-two pieces.
limit: A signal game records a learning format. It does not independently document a live signal exchange.
firstAction: Turn the toy’s window to expose the practice flag.
firstView: A flag appears through one paper aperture. The folded cue is still beneath the rim.
secondAction: Stop the wheel at its second marked view and raise the matching piece.
secondView: The second flag appears with its independent token. The trainer can reset the wheel for the next person.
returnEvidence: The upper watch will practise a fictional flag sequence. The lower porter needs confirmation when they cannot see it.
high: Send a training turn to the sighted watch post.
low: Carry the printed reply to the lower rail.

title: Folding white-and-blue ball signal
summary: This ship-to-ship signal consists of silk on two metal ovals, which lie flat for storage and pivot open.
limit: The folded silhouette does not reproduce the form a receiving crew would see.
firstAction: Raise the two paper ovals until both are visible.
firstView: From the intended spot the study signal fills its opening. At the side the overlap looks narrow.
secondAction: Fold down the front oval and turn the viewer’s arrow.
secondView: The occupied window shrinks. The result is a different cue despite using the same two pieces.
returnEvidence: The first receiver sees a narrow practice shape behind the wall and a second receiver sees the mounted form from a clear line.
high: Confirm the open shape from the seaward position.
low: Leave the low crew a shape reply with an edge-view warning.

title: Greenwich Observatory’s red Time Ball
summary: The Maudslay, Sons & Field ball first signalled time in 1833. Its high place made it available to Thames crews and other viewers.
limit: The visible drop serves people with a sightline. A separate handover still matters when the view is blocked.
firstAction: Drop the marked paper token behind the low screen.
firstView: The lower receiver sees no motion through the wall. The visible slot stays blank.
secondAction: Raise the token to the high window and let it pass.
secondView: The upper receiver sees the changed mark and can give the place and moment independently.
returnEvidence: One crew needs a high view. Another is on the lower deck stack. A single signal cannot serve both positions in the same way.
high: Check the drop mark at the upper sight line.
low: Confirm delivery by the lower runner and record why.

title: Hubert Airy’s drawing of the fallen time ball
summary: Airy drew the ball after it fell into the courtyard in December 1855 and inscribed the date of the fall.
limit: A drawing of a fallen signal can document the failure. It does not record the timing of the normal drop.
firstAction: Put the ball token in the yard slot instead of the clock slot.
firstView: The yard now has a dated failure record. The normal timing space is still empty.
secondAction: Clip the independent watch time beside its own mark.
secondView: The watch strip remains a separate source from the drawing of the failure.
returnEvidence: Anwen needs instructions during a missed practice signal. The failed cue itself is worth recording apart from the clock.
high: Put a failed signal card in the upper lookout’s check.
low: Send the watch time by the lower runner without treating it as a normal drop.

title: Morris and Mapple’s hourly time signal relay
summary: The relay was added to the Royal Observatory time apparatus to take work previously handled by the ball detent.
limit: A relay output can share its source with the original cue. It is not an independently set clock.
firstAction: Connect the model’s short output ribbon to the parent cue.
firstView: Two counters change after the same plate moves. The receiving ribbon has no separate origin mark.
secondAction: Open the separately numbered local receipt.
secondView: It has its own time entry. The two driven counters still share one source.
returnEvidence: Two bells ring at the quay for one shift. The keeper wants to know whether the second bell can confirm the first.
high: Post the shared source with its two outputs at the lookout.
low: Fit the independently signed receipt to the runner’s board.

title: Hancocks and Co. time-signal apparatus
summary: The catalogue connects this apparatus with the history of time signals sent by telegraph from Greenwich.
limit: The original dispatch and a receiver’s own acknowledgement provide different evidence.
firstAction: Set the sender slip in the outgoing compartment.
firstView: The source transmits once. No acknowledgment has yet been filed.
secondAction: Move the separate receiving slip onto the hooked rack.
secondView: The delivery now has a time at the receiving end and a separate issue time.
returnEvidence: The harbour uses a rule requiring the other end to acknowledge the next practice handover.
high: Send the out-time code to the lookout to compare with its log.
low: Fit the waiting place and the actual receipt below the rail.

title: Meteorological Office Ships’ Code Card
summary: This folded card sets out the code for meteorological observations sent by radio.
limit: A code card can translate a message. It does not supply the observation or prove that the message arrived.
firstAction: Lay the folded practice key beside the outgoing slip.
firstView: The outgoing marks can be copied. Their meanings need the matching key.
secondAction: Turn the key to its open inner face.
secondView: The pretend marks can be read by the second keeper. The original observation slot stays separate.
returnEvidence: Anwen’s crew can use a key to interpret the practice strip. The weather still needs a marked time and place.
high: Carry the interpreted symbols with a source place.
low: Leave the code and the independent observed entry on paired hooks.

title: Code card for auxiliary ships and other weather reporters
summary: The UK Met Office card distinguishes subsidiary reporting groups, including reports marked MARID for sea-surface temperature.
limit: A shared radio channel does not make every vessel’s report the same kind of observation.
firstAction: Clip the painted boat-class tab above the fictional message.
firstView: The observer writes a class tag before the figures pass on.
secondAction: Slide the special water-report mark into its own opening.
secondView: The receiver now sees which observation type to file without filling in the others.
returnEvidence: The harbour office receives two reports over the same channel. The tag decides which actual practice tray receives each.
high: Signal the named class to the lookout’s separate tray.
low: Carry the narrowly labelled water reading to the lower receiver.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Bolivar Point Fresnel lighthouse lens
date: Late 19th century; recorded hurricane use 16–17 August 1917
summary: This Smithsonian lens came from Bolivar Point. The record includes the lighthouse’s August 1917 use during a hurricane.
limit: A lens design’s date and the date a particular installation served its watch are separate. The original field performance was wider than this paper model.
firstAction: Move a printed light stripe across the open study window.
firstView: The stripe passes through a single opening. Its position stays on the strip.
secondAction: Put the position tag beside the drawn weather frame.
secondView: The observation conditions receive their own tag. No number for distance has been added.
returnEvidence: A lower pier keeper needs to record visibility during a particular watch. The same design can be used in other weather without promising the same range.
high: Carry the named window test to the upper walk.
low: Mount the watch conditions on a lower accessible card.

title: James Douglass’s twin-wick lightship burner
summary: The museum describes the burner and metal reflector as lightvessel equipment. Units of the type continued as standby sources after being replaced as main lights.
limit: A working backup and a record of which source was running answer different questions.
firstAction: Swap the two printed source strips on the light model.
firstView: The same sight opening lights in the model when the replacement source strip is slid into place.
secondAction: Lift the paper backup notice while the public opening remains.
secondView: The watcher sees which source is meant to be running. The light position has not told them that alone.
returnEvidence: The lookout at the old quay can pass a visible signal while the clerk notes which study source provided it.
high: Share the observed signal at the high lookout.
low: File the separately named backup source at the lower rail.

title: Lightship’s chain-driven clock mechanism
summary: The drive turned a light used in a lightvessel. The museum qualifies the identity of the vessel believed to have used this mechanism.
limit: A recorded function does not confirm the individual ship associated with a loose mechanism.
firstAction: Set an interval strip above the toy rotating light pattern.
firstView: There are two repeats of the same model trace. The vessel-name slot stays blank.
secondAction: Bring the proposed vessel tag to the separate intake drawer.
secondView: It sits under a qualified heading. The repeated light pattern does not change.
returnEvidence: The incoming display draft names a practice vessel more firmly than its receipt allows. Keep the functioning part while preserving the open custody line.
high: Take the repeat pattern to the lookout without a firm ship name.
low: Fit the tentative vessel tag into the separately headed lower sleeve.

title: Henry P. Bird’s photograph of Don Cameron on Relume
summary: The colour transparency shows chief engineer Don Cameron at work in Relume’s control room.
limit: A still photograph can locate a person and place without proving which equipment change happened next.
firstAction: Frame the printed study silhouette beside the console outline.
firstView: The position of a pictured worker can be marked. The next action remains off the frame.
secondAction: Move the later handover slip under its separate tab.
secondView: A second note can tell the next shift what happened. The practice picture did not supply it.
returnEvidence: The harbour has a drawing of its morning keeper near the practice signal. The relay crew needs an independently reported next action.
high: Carry the pictured working position to the watch crew.
low: Fit the dated second handover slip below the picture.

title: Clyde Shipping brochure with Copeland accommodation receipt
summary: The brochure contains a foldout deck plan and a separate inserted accommodation receipt for SS Copeland.
limit: A plan shows possible spaces. A receipt records one transaction, without establishing how every space was used.
firstAction: Open the foldout and put the inserted slip in its own tray.
firstView: The route has several spaces. One separate numbered leaf records a transaction.
secondAction: Match the slip’s date tag to its narrow named space.
secondView: The purchased space receives an entry. Others stay open.
returnEvidence: The caretaker wants to show a visitor where a cabin is. The booking clerk needs the specific receipt before certifying its use.
high: Carry the general position plan to the lookout.
low: Deliver the actual receipt to the lower ledger clerk.

title: Mauretania maiden-voyage postcard with log abstract
summary: The rear of this colour postcard gives an abstract of the voyage from New York, including journey information and weather.
limit: The selected summary cannot supply every watch entry from the more detailed underlying log.
firstAction: Turn the mock card from its picture to its short log extract.
firstView: The extract has time and weather headings. Unchosen watch slots remain blank.
secondAction: Set the fuller observation card beside the postcard.
secondView: The reader can file one extra watch under its own source instead of assuming the extract supplied it.
returnEvidence: A visitor wants a readable journey summary and a later researcher wants the original watch detail. Keep the role of the extract visible.
high: Take the short journey card with the empty-watch note.
low: File the summary and longer working log separately on the lower rail.

title: Liverpool pilotage rates and law abstract
summary: The broadside groups vessels and gives different Liverpool pilotage rates alongside a summary of rules.
limit: The printed tariff shows categories used by the authority. It does not show that any individual vessel paid a particular rate.
firstAction: Put the fictional tariff card under the visible category labels.
firstView: The tariff is legible, but there is no payment mark for the waiting boat.
secondAction: Lay a separate receipt beneath the named category.
secondView: The payment entry can now travel with the right case. Other vessel rows stay untouched.
returnEvidence: The harbour's fictional pilotage notice is public. One crew wants to check whether its receipt was filed under the assigned category.
high: Display the category guide with its scope, separate from paid receipts.
low: Take the actual marked payment row to the keeper’s lower tray.

title: Selected Ship’s Meteorological Logbook
summary: The Met Office designed this form for Selected ships, whose crews used several instruments and sent coded observations on a set schedule.
limit: A printed field identifies an expected kind of observation. A blank field is not a zero measurement.
firstAction: Set the practice log under the blank weather row frame.
firstView: The headings stay visible. There has been no recorded reading on the blank row.
secondAction: Attach the separately witnessed surface entry under its proper heading.
secondView: Only its own row is now filled.
returnEvidence: A look-out has returned one observation. The rest of the form can stay recoverable without pretending the values were measured.
high: Send the one completed row to the high board.
low: Send the whole form with blanks marked for a future watch.

title: Supplementary Ship’s Meteorological Logbook
summary: The Met Office assigned this form to its Supplementary reporting class in the voluntary observing fleet.
limit: Two forms with similar headings can have different reporting scopes, instruments or expectations.
firstAction: Fit the supplementary title onto the practice table.
firstView: One category has a place for its own observation. The other form’s slots cannot be assumed.
secondAction: Raise the independent issue slip from the drawer.
secondView: It ties this form to the right class and leaves the contents for a crew report.
returnEvidence: The shore sorter has two model packet families. Train the next keeper to preserve the actual class before joining comparisons.
high: Carry the scope title to the upper receiver.
low: File the class slip with the local report in the lower tray.

title: Tear-off pad for British ships’ radio weather reports
summary: The Met Office produced the pad of printed telegram forms for reporting weather from volunteer observing ships.
limit: A sent form and a received message can be linked, but copies are not independent observations.
firstAction: Tear off a paper practice copy along the rule.
firstView: The two leaves preserve one entry with the same dispatch identifier.
secondAction: Put a separate observer’s entry on an independent hook.
secondView: The observer recorded a separate checked mark. The two copied leaves remain one source.
returnEvidence: The two returned slips agree because a single dispatch made both. One checker adds their independently signed report.
high: Take the matching trace copies with a common-source note.
low: Pair one dispatch with the independent quay witness.

title: William Hay Wardrop’s two coastline drawings
summary: The two pen-and-ink views form part of a dated logbook entry, later mounted in an album.
limit: Mounting gives both images a common album address. It does not guarantee they depict the same point or moment.
firstAction: Attach the common log date tab above both practice views.
firstView: Each view keeps its own corner cross. Neither copied line is allowed to cover the other.
secondAction: Raise the album sleeve while keeping the pair codes nearby.
secondView: The position of this leaf changes in the filing system. Its log date remains in place.
returnEvidence: The lookout can try one rehearsal picture against a view. The receiving archivist needs the common date and the two separate view marks.
high: Use one clearly marked view at the upper quay.
low: File both angles under their common dated entry.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: E. & G. W. Blunt sextant linked to Theodorus B. M. Mason
summary: The silvered-scale sextant is marked E. & G. W. Blunt. The record qualifies when Mason likely acquired it and names his sister as donor.
limit: A probable acquisition date and the actual gift record should remain separate.
firstAction: Seat the name-marked practice plate in the equipment tray.
firstView: The maker mark is visible. It does not date Mason’s receipt.
secondAction: Set the dated donor line on its own shelf under the earlier attribution.
secondView: Both people have named roles. The probable purchase retains its qualifier.
returnEvidence: The harbour crew can file a direct custody record even when it still has to qualify the earlier owner’s date.
high: Take the visible maker mark to the mounted index.
low: Carry known donor and probable owner on separate cards.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: S. Thaxter & Son nautical compass with Robert King paper card
summary: The gimbal-mounted compass bears more than one trade name. Robert King is named on the paper card and the record lists S. Thaxter & Son as maker.
limit: An inscription may identify the card, maker or seller. It cannot automatically stand for every part.
firstAction: Lift the practice card out of the open copied bowl.
firstView: The ring shows its name in one place. The outer bowl retains its separate label.
secondAction: Lay the two named pieces together without covering their tags.
secondView: A second reader can recover both roles while still seeing one mounted instrument.
returnEvidence: One harbour case has two names on one article. Save the part each name belongs to in the catalogue line.
high: Carry the active dial alongside the card’s proper attribution.
low: Post both component names in two readable slots.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Ritchie liquid compass documented in the maker’s ledger
summary: The Ritchie ledger records its making and sale to T. S. & J. D. Negus. The object later belonged to the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey.
limit: The maker’s ledger and later institutional ownership describe different custody events.
firstAction: Put the manufacture date stamp on the top practice slip.
firstView: The date goes with making. The sale and later custody rows remain independent.
secondAction: Match the later keeper stamp to its separately sourced entry.
secondView: The first date survives in place while the later institution has its own line.
returnEvidence: The model’s two entry stamps turn out to belong to different owners. A borrower needs the later association while the keeper keeps the maker record.
high: Take the correctly limited maker page to the upper index.
low: Clip the separate ownership progression into the lower ledger.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: Marine Compass Company compass from Alcoa Mariner’s lifeboat
summary: The museum reports that the compass was used in a lifeboat from the Alcoa Mariner in September 1942. Hodges gave it to the Smithsonian.
limit: The known lifeboat use does not give every sailor’s experience of the event.
firstAction: Set the donated compass card beside the place-of-use tag.
firstView: The keeper can identify the lifeboat without adding a crew member’s words.
secondAction: Slot the named donor line below the catalogue date.
secondView: The human record now names the donor and keeps unused testimony boxes blank.
returnEvidence: The next harbour keeper can verify the donated item and the stated role. Respect the voices absent from the current catalogue.
high: Mount the sourced use card at the upper check.
low: Put the donor link next to the quiet open testimony slot.

institution: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
title: William Chambers’s The Universal Navigator
summary: The book describes several navigation methods, including instrument, tabular and geometric approaches.
limit: Multiple methods described together need not yield independent evidence if they use the same inputs.
firstAction: Clip the practice geometry and table examples above one source mark.
firstView: Two representations can recover the same exercise result. One input slip feeds both.
secondAction: Give a second independent slip its own origin line.
secondView: The extra observation can now be checked apart from the repeated calculation.
returnEvidence: The old harbour trial can use two calculation formats. The crew’s separate report can provide a distinct source.
high: Carry a readable method sheet with the shared input named.
low: Keep the second independent mark with its own source line.
